en: If you are angry with me, I bow to you; yet this state of being bowed to should not be bowed down to by you.
This quality of being bowed to shines in you through your royal nature, as I consider you to be like a great king.
Because it extends even to jars and other such objects, the probans (sādhana) stated by you is inconclusive (sādhāraṇa).
May Rāma, who was thus defeated by his beloved in their verbal sparring, grant you happiness.
"Kṛṣṇa shall nourish your happiness; O fair-faced one, become cheerful! Go, go to that beloved of yours.
Why do you sully me, who am attached to another, O dear one? It is solely due to your own nature.
"If such is your simplicity, then this [accusation] is a unique cause for only one side [of the argument]."
May He, consoling Rādhikā—who had been quarreling with Him in love—by saying "because of your virtuous conduct," grant you prosperity.
Every object brings you happiness; then from where does this pain of yours come, that you speak thus of this world as being composed of that [suffering]?
This reason is inconclusive because of the absence of the two examples. This is the [point].
May the conversation of the Lord of Sītā with Lakṣmaṇa while he was separated from her protect you.
"I am terrified and separated from the moon; yet here it rises!
How is this known to you, since it causes me such intense torment?
"Who infers [the moon's rise] from a mark that is pervaded by its absence from the probandum? This is merely your folly."
"Do not fear"—thus was the Lord of the Raghus consoled by the son of Sumitrā; may he protect you.
O Lord of the Raghus, what fear do you have of the moon? Because it is the maker of night (the source of faults), it is attached to afflicting others like a slanderer—why is this not said?
This reason is countered by a valid counter-argument, since it [the moon] abides in virtuous conduct.
May Rāghava, whose fear has been dispelled by his brother, nourish you with happiness.
"This suffering of separation is false; this illusory Maithilī maiden standing before you is truly real as your beloved.
Thus addressed by his innate friend in the art of consolation, he took refuge in this very reason.
May the beloved of Śrī Jānakī protect you, demonstrating his state of perfection.
My mind, born of the mind, pierces me with its arrows; who could destroy that which has itself as its own locus?
Because of the mind's grossness, what indeed does it not do when it functions without discernment? They say the mind is atomic in size; how then can there be such grossness in its very nature?
This reason is thus established; may it protect the conversation between the two sons of Daśaratha for you.
Śuka and Sāraṇa should not be killed, for there is indeed no quality of being fit for execution in them;
because they are Rākṣasas, like the Ten-necked One (Rāvaṇa) and others—this reason is qualified by a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Here, "being treacherous" (*sadrohatva*) is easily understood as the limiting condition; you should consider the remainder.
May the illustrious Rāghava, who thus shattered the arguments of the son of Āditya, protect you!
"O Rāghava, this [demon] is conquerable by humans; he cannot be harmed by *yātudhānas* who subsist on him. This reason was indeed stated based on direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).
But where is this direct perception? [It is found] before his elder brother when he says, "He has slain Khara and the others."
May Rāghava, whose very name is proclaimed as a source of terror by those who hold opposing views, grant you happiness.

"O beautiful lady, not knowing what is in your heart, how can I ask for your desired wish? Surely you may infer from this glance alone that there is passion in my heart. If you say this, it is not so; for this reason is fallacious due to a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and in this case, the heavy burden of shame is that very limiting condition.
Indeed, that [quality] pervades the probandum in the case of a beloved woman and so forth, yet it does not pervade the means [of proof] at the front of battle.
The crown prince Mahākavi, a resident of Koṭiliṅgapura,
has set forth the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) in ten verses for the delight of the virtuous.
